title: Non-Invasive Molecular Biomarkers in Colorectal Cancer: Pathogenic Mechanisms, Clinical Relevance, and Pathology Diagnosis
content: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major global public health concern, ranking as the third most frequently diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Its development is associated with the accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations that promote the transformation of colorectal polyps into malignant tumors. The main molecular mechanisms involved include chromosomal instability (CIN), microsatellite instability (MSI), and the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), together with alterations in signaling pathways such as Wnt and genes including APC and RAS. Early diagnosis is essential to improve patient prognosis and survival. In this context, identifying molecular biomarkers in non-invasive biological samples, such as blood and stool, represents a promising strategy for early detection, tumor progression monitoring, and prediction of therapeutic responses. Particular emphasis is placed and discusses classical and non-classical DNA- and RNA-based biomarkers, including MACC1, c-MYC, ITGA6, SDC2, CEACAM5, APC, SEPT9, MLH1, and CDKN2A. These biomarkers demonstrate potential utility for early detection, risk stratification, prognosis, and monitoring of recurrence. We discuss their molecular functions, clinical relevance, and feasibility in non-invasive testing strategies. Integrating validated biomarkers into multi-target panels may enhance early diagnosis and support personalized therapeutic decision-making, ultimately improving patient outcomes in colorectal cancer.
